description:
It is always a real  thrill for me to see ducks in the wild, and I would say that in this region, I encounter Wood Ducks actually more often than any other species, even Mallards, when I am away from places that people frequent (such as parks and stocked fishing lakes). They are, however, ducks that like their privacy, and it is rare for me to get a close view of them. A small group of ducks of some sort (2 to 4 perhaps) flew noisily away from me twice along this stretch of Enlow Fork, but not such that I could get a clear photo of them. None of those made any sounds like the "quacks" of Mallards in any case. Maybe Teal? I couldn't tell. 

Then I spotted this female Wood Duck on the creek about 55 meters (180 feet) away, and she pretty calmly allowed me to watch her swim and climb up on a rock for more than a minute, before paddling off downstream. She did not make a sound or fly. 

This was on a fairly remote section of the Enlow Fork of Wheeling Creek, which carves a deep twisting narrow valley through the Allegheny Plateau and its mixed deciduous (Maple-Oak-Beech-Hickory etc.) woodlands, here at an elevation around 264 meters (866 feet).

description:
The photographs I barely managed to quickly snap in the evening shade are not up to my usual standards for posting on *iNaturalist*, and I hope for better ones here in future, but when I checked online, I found that Ducks are not well represented in this locality in *iNaturalist* reports, so I  will use these sub-par pics this time anyway. 

These two Wood Ducks took to the air as soon as they heard me coming and were gone within seconds. At least one I believe is female. They had been on the water at the upper shallow end of a little pond half covered in lilly pads that has only just recently been improved for County Park visitors with a footpath cleared around it and a park bench to sit on next to an informational signpost. It seems the Ducks were enjoying the quiet right under a newly erected Wood Duck size nesting box. Perhaps they were scouting out next year's accommodations. I think this part of the Park has so far received fewer visitors than along the main creek in the valley where there are beautifully maintained paths and pavilions. In any case, it seems this is a first *iNat'* observation of Wood Ducks in *Mingo Creek County Park* so far. I'm very happy to see that they have found this little out of the way pond, and thank the Park staff for putting up the nesting box as well. Ponds are such valuable attractions for *so* many kinds of wildlife. 

These fast flying Ducks were on this small pond surrounded by mixed deciduous woodland with a few nearby patches of planted evergreens and a few surrounding farms, on a slope below the hilltop and a nearby paved road, at an elevation around 334 meters (1096 feet) according to an old USGS Topographic map. I will definitely be keeping my eye on this charming corner of the Park.

With Christine Rowland, Klenisson Brenner, and Lilian Saul & Doug Wassmer; a welcome trip to this always popular spot. All of us needed Canvasback for a Polk County bird -- and Klenisson needed it for a lifer. There is one present (I guess according to eBird), but we did not find it, despite 15 minutes of scanning every duck in the Aythya flock. The weather at the start was sunny and 56 degrees ("feels like" 53), with a light breeze. We encircled the lake and then left at 1344, heading home.

Concerning the Mallards, other than 2 that were obvious hybrids with Muscovy Ducks, I am calling all of them Domestic Mallards; I did not see anything diagnostic for a hybrid/back-cross with Mottled Duck.

The male.

description:
Wilson Springs Ponds are lined on one bank with Russian olive trees. Having only seen wood ducks on the water, I was intrigued to see wood ducks in the trees eating the berries. I learned that a times, dozens of wood ducks roost in the trees.

Besides the berries, the trees also contain lost fishing lures. While I was visiting, members of the local fire department were wading about on the other side of the water and called out to me if I could see a duck caught in a tree. They'd received a call reporting a stuck duck. Sure enough, just around the bend, a drake wood duck was hanging by a wing, flapping in place. A fireman located the bird and gently cut it loose. Sadly, the fireman said this was not an isolated incident.
I believe they are wood ducks. They showed up the morning after the February frost.

description:
A solo visit, rather last-minute. There was a report the night before about 2230 on the main Florida birding Facebook group about a possible Tufted Duck at Lake Morton in Lakeland. I decided to chase it. This morning, by 0730, before I left, two European birders had commented that the duck was a hybrid, with Tufted Duck being one parent and either a Ring-necked Duck or a Lesser Scaup being the other parent. Clearly, this news massively dampened enthusiasm for chasing the duck. I'm sure that 60+ birders who had packed their cars last night had decided to stay home once the duck was identified as a hybrid. Birders can be funny about that oftentimes ... I decided to chase the duck regardless, since it was reasonably close (less than a 90-minute drive), I had nothing else planned today, and it's always fun to see all the swans, geese, and other exotic waterfowl -- and the native species too. I arrived at 1030 and the ONLY other birder present was John Cima, who had discovered the duck about a week ago. If not for the two posts this morning, probably 100 birders would have descended on the park today. The weather at the start was sunny and 67 degrees ("feels like" 67) with a light breeze. When I left at 1230, it was sunny and low 70s with a light breeze.

I parked at the southeastern corner of the lake and walked  counter-clockwise, since the light was better than walking clockwise. I _tried_ to tally every individual of every bird species present, but it is nearly impossible given the amount of birds and the fact that I was concentrating (as always) of photographing as many birds as I could.

My camera, a Panasonic Lumix FZ80 (my sixth, I think) quit working yesterday; the camera turns off when I try to zoom in (it has 60x, zoom, which I use to the maximum). It's still under warranty, so I need to send it back. To my surprise, returning home yesterday, I found an old Lumix FZ80 (maybe my fifth) that I had forgotten about, sitting on a shelf in my closet. The exposure knob no longer functions -- a known defect with this camera model, in my experience -- but a faulty camera with a functioning 60x, zoom is 1,000,000 times better than no camera or a camera with no functioning zoom.

The first few dozen images I took today, in bright sunlight in my standard "Intelligent Auto" setting, were quite dark (the exposure "broke" in a very dark setting). I deleted most of these images, since I do not believe in editing images (other than cropping) that I upload to iNat. I experimented with other settings. To my surprise and delight, the "SCN" setting -- for scene selection -- proved to be a wonderful alternative, taking images that were beautiful in shade and only slightly (at times) overexposed in direct sunlight. Overall, I was quite pleased with this camera today -- I took more than 1,200 photographs here and at Colt Creek State Park, where I visited after leaving Lakeland!

If I have posted multiple records of a species, then I am positive or nearly certain that they represent multiple individuals. Selected bird species and estinmated numbers at Lake Morton Park follow:

White Ibis: 300+, with 95% in adult plumage

Mallard: I quit counting quickly, but I estimate 75-100 in a typically massive degree of variation in plumages. I did not see any Mallards that I thought were back-crosses with Mottled Ducks, but I marked two males as "Mallards, Pintails, and Allies."

Mute Swan: 35-40, with two active nests with eggs

Black Swan: 20-25, with 2 nests with eggs and a pair with two cygnets. NOTE: why can't I "count" the eggs or cygets as wild birds from "captive" parents? According to iNaturalist guidelines referencing captive plants or animals, the progengy of these individuals should be "countable" and Research-Gradable. Right? Or wrong?

American White Pelican: 60, mostly in one flock. At one point, a dozen or more individuals fed in a flock literally along the shoreline, less than 15 feet from where I was standing, taking videos. American White Pelicans are noisy when foraging!

Swan Goose: 1, seemingly not a hybrid/back-cross.

Graylag Goose: 1, seemingly not a hybrid/back-cross.

I did not see either of the two Black-necked Swans or the single Coscoroba Swan that were present in previous years; apparently they are now dead.

I took a ton of photographs of the putative Tufted Duck hybrid. Additional comments on Facebook since I took my photographs suggest that the duck may simply be a very worn female Lesser Scaup. Accordingly, I am listing it as "Scaups, Pochards, and Allies."
